the method used to measure the follow-up time of antidepressant treatment in the studies mentioned is biased and that the bias leads to a protective effect of longer antidepressant use.
measurement of follow up time in observational studies can be subject to two types of bias: immortal and neglected.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the methodological problems in the measurement of time to relapse in the context of antidepressant treatment.
the influence of the measurement of time on the risk of relapse of depression for antidepressant users.
the influence of measurement of follow-up on the risk of relapse of depression for antidepressant users with early discontinuation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is insufficient evidence for the effectiveness of long-term treatment with antidepressants.
longer treatment duration does not reduce the risk of relapse/ recurrence of depression.
longer treatments may not be associated with a lower risk of relapse/ recurrence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no evidence for an association between the duration of treatment and the risk of recurrence/ relapse of depression.
the risk of recurrence/ relapse for patients who discontiue antidepressant use is similar to that for patients who continue antidepressant use.
the duration of antidepressant use does not protect against recurrence/relapse, and discontinuation of use does not increase risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk ratio for relapse/recurrence of early discontinuers versus continuing users depends on the method used to measure time.
the method used to measure follow-up time can lead to different results.
the method used to measure follow-up time can influence the results.
